Sharp Rogers–Shephard Inequalities
for Rényi Entropy

Bang-Xian Han    Guoqing Zhan    Chiyu Zhou    Zhuo-Nan Zhu ††thanks: Bang-Xian Han is with the School of Mathematics, Shandong University, Jinan 250100, China (e-mail: hanbx@sdu.edu.cn).††thanks: Guoqing Zhan is with the School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China (e-mail: zhanguoqing@mail.ustc.edu.cn).††thanks: Chiyu Zhou is with the School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China (e-mail: dovong@mail.ustc.edu.cn).††thanks: Zhuo-Nan Zhu is with the School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China (e-mail: zhuonanzhu@mail.ustc.edu.cn).
Abstract

We establish sharp weighted Rogers–Shephard inequalities for Rényi differential entropy. For independent copies X,X′X,X^{\prime} of a log-concave random vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we prove hp​(a​X−b​X′)≤hp​(X)+n​log⁡(a+b)h_{p}(aX-bX^{\prime})\leq h_{p}(X)+n\log(a+b) for all a,b>0a,b>0 and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, where orders 11 and ∞\infty correspond to Shannon entropy and min-entropy, respectively. The Shannon case settles the entropic Rogers–Shephard conjecture of Madiman and Kontoyiannis and its higher-dimensional formulation. For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, equality holds precisely for invertible affine images of random vectors with independent exponential coordinates. At p=∞p=\infty, the larger equality class is characterized by possibly extended-valued convex potentials that are positively homogeneous of degree one. For every 0<p<10<p<1, uniform laws on sufficiently high-dimensional simplices violate the unweighted bound. Thus p=1p=1 is the critical order for this bound to hold in every dimension. The proof combines weighted convex intersections with an exponential lift to a log-affine probability density. At the Shannon endpoint, this lift yields an exact deficit decomposition with a conditional mutual information term for an additive channel with asymmetric Laplace noise.

Index Terms: 
Conditional mutual information, log-concavity, Rényi entropy, Rogers–Shephard inequality, Ruzsa divergence

I Introduction

We study entropy growth when an independent copy of a random vector is subtracted from it. For a random vector XX with density ff on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, its Shannon differential entropy is

h(X)=h(f)=−∫ℝnf(x)logf(x)dx.h(X)=h(f)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x)\log f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.

Densities and integrals without an indicated measure are with respect to Lebesgue measure. All logarithms are natural and we use the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. This entropy has the opposite sign to the functional ∫f​log⁡f\int f\log f commonly used in optimal transport.

We ask for the sharp upper bound on h⁡(X−X′)−h⁡(X)h(X-X^{\prime})-h(X) when X′X^{\prime} is an independent copy of a log-concave random vector XX. In the continuous setting, log-concavity means that XX has a log-concave Lebesgue density; its support has nonempty interior. For a uniform law on a convex body, the classical Rogers–Shephard inequality [1] bounds the volume of the support of the difference. Entropy depends on the entire convolution density, so a sharp entropy bound requires more than control of the support. This upper-bound problem complements the lower bounds supplied by the entropy power inequality [2, 3, 4]. We determine the sharp upper bound under log-concavity and characterize all laws attaining it.

The problem also has an additive-combinatorial background in Ruzsa’s sumset calculus and the study of additive representation functions and additive energy. Inequalities for sumset and difference-set sizes have entropy counterparts for independent sums and differences. Madiman and Kontoyiannis [5] developed this connection through the Ruzsa divergence for random vectors and, more generally, random variables on locally compact Polish abelian groups. More recently, Li, Gavalakis and Kontoyiannis [6] introduced entropic additive energy for continuous random variables and established entropy inequalities for sums, products, and sum-product combinations. This representation viewpoint directs attention to the full difference distribution and its entropy. We write I⁡(U,W)I(U;W) for mutual information: if U,WU,W have joint density fU,Wf_{U,W} and marginal densities fU,fWf_{U},f_{W}, then

I⁡(U,W)=∫fU,W​(u,w)​log⁡fU,W​(u,w)fU​(u)​fW​(w)​𝑑u​𝑑w,I(U;W)=\int f_{U,W}(u,w)\log\frac{f_{U,W}(u,w)}{f_{U}(u)f_{W}(w)}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}w,

with zero integrand wherever fU,W=0f_{U,W}=0. For a log-concave random vector XX and an independent copy X′X^{\prime}, the Ruzsa divergence of XX from itself is

dR(X∥X)=h(X−X′)−h(X)=I(X−X′;X′),d_{R}(X\|X)=h(X-X^{\prime})-h(X)=I(X-X^{\prime};X^{\prime}), (1)

where the last equality in (1) follows by conditioning on X′X^{\prime} and using translation invariance of differential entropy. The entropy power inequality yields dR(X∥X)≥(n/2)log2d_{R}(X\|X)\geq(n/2)\log 2.

Madiman and Kontoyiannis [5, Corollaries 9 and 10] proved dR(X∥X)≤2nlog2d_{R}(X\|X)\leq 2n\log 2 for log-concave laws and conjectured the sharp constant log⁡2\log 2 in dimension one, with one-sided exponentials as the only extremizers [5, Conjecture 1]. Melbourne and Tkocz [7, Section VI] formulated the dimension-nn conjecture and proved its Rényi counterpart for orders p≥2p\geq 2.

I-A The Shannon and Ruzsa bounds

Theorem 1 (Sharp Shannon bound)

Let X,X′X,X^{\prime} be independent random vectors with the same log-concave probability density on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then

n2​log⁡2≤h⁡(X−X′)−h⁡(X)≤n​log⁡2.\frac{n}{2}\log 2\leq h(X-X^{\prime})-h(X)\leq n\log 2. (2)

Equality in the lower bound holds if and only if XX is a nondegenerate Gaussian random vector. Equality in the upper bound holds if and only if XX is an invertible affine image of a random vector with independent one-sided exponential coordinates. Equivalently, 2≤N⁡(X−X′)/N⁡(X)≤42\leq N(X-X^{\prime})/N(X)\leq 4, where N⁡(X)=(2​π​e)−1​e2​h​(X)/nN(X)=(2\pi e)^{-1}e^{2h(X)/n} is the entropy power.

The lower bound and its equality cases follow from the entropy power inequality, while the upper bound settles the conjecture discussed above. In terms of Ruzsa divergence, this gives the following corollary.

Corollary 2 (Ruzsa divergence)

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1,

n2log2≤dR(X∥X)=I(X−X′;X′)≤nlog2,\frac{n}{2}\log 2\leq d_{R}(X\|X)=I(X-X^{\prime};X^{\prime})\leq n\log 2, (3)

with the same equality cases as in Theorem 1. The difference constant of [5, Definition 4] therefore satisfies

1≤σ−​(X):=N⁡(X−X′)2​N​(X)≤2.1\leq\sigma_{-}(X):=\frac{N(X-X^{\prime})}{2N(X)}\leq 2. (4)

This sharpens the upper bound on dR(X∥X)d_{R}(X\|X) in [5, Corollary 10].

I-B The full Rényi range and equality cases

For a probability density ff on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, the Rényi differential entropy [8] of order p∈(0,1)∪(1,∞)p\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty), together with its Shannon and min-entropy limits, is given by

hp(f)=11−plog∫ℝnf(x)pdx,h1(f)=h(f),h∞(f)=−log∥f∥∞.\displaystyle h_{p}(f)=\frac{1}{1-p}\log\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x)^{p}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad h_{1}(f)=h(f),\qquad h_{\infty}(f)=-\log\|f\|_{\infty}. (5)

For a random vector XX with density ff, we also write hp​(X)=hp​(f)h_{p}(X)=h_{p}(f). We call h∞h_{\infty} the min-entropy. Except in the discrete discussion in Section VIII-B, entropy means differential entropy. Melbourne and Tkocz [7, Theorem VI.1] proved

hp​(X−X′)≤hp​(X)+n​log⁡2,2≤p≤∞.h_{p}(X-X^{\prime})\leq h_{p}(X)+n\log 2,\qquad 2\leq p\leq\infty. (6)

Their argument combines the identity

h∞​(X−X′)=h2​(X)h_{\infty}(X-X^{\prime})=h_{2}(X) (7)

with sharp comparisons between Rényi entropies of log-concave densities [9, 10, 11]. For integrable functions u,vu,v, write (u∗v)​(x)=∫u⁡(x−y)​v​(y)​𝑑y(u*v)(x)=\int u(x-y)v(y)\,\mathrm{d}y for their convolution, and let f~​(x)=f​(−x)\widetilde{f}(x)=f(-x) denote the reflection of ff. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, (f∗f~)​(0)=∫f2=‖f∗f~‖∞(f*\widetilde{f})(0)=\int f^{2}=\|f*\widetilde{f}\|_{\infty}, which proves (7).

For 0<p<20<p<2, the same comparison method bounds the entropy increment by n​log⁡p/(p−1)n\log p/(p-1), interpreted as nn at p=1p=1. This Shannon bound is due to Bobkov and Madiman [12] and also follows from [9]. In dimension one, Melbourne, Nayar and Roberto [13, Corollary 2.3] obtain the stronger bound h⁡(X−X′)−h⁡(X)≤12​log⁡(4​π/e)h(X-X^{\prime})-h(X)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(4\pi/e) from their sharp lower bound on entropy at fixed variance. The remaining problem is the sharp bound for 1≤p<21\leq p<2, including the Shannon endpoint. We prove it in every dimension and allow arbitrary positive weights.

Theorem 3 (Weighted Rényi bound)

Let X,X′X,X^{\prime} be independent random vectors with the same log-concave probability density on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then, for every a,b>0a,b>0 and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty,

hp​(a​X−b​X′)≤hp​(X)+n​log⁡(a+b).h_{p}(aX-bX^{\prime})\leq h_{p}(X)+n\log(a+b). (8)

All entropies in (8) are finite. The constant is optimal for each choice of n,p,a,bn,p,a,b.

In particular, taking a=b=1/2a=b=1/2, we obtain

hp​(X−X′2)≤hp​(X),1≤p≤∞,h_{p}\left(\frac{X-X^{\prime}}{2}\right)\leq h_{p}(X),\qquad 1\leq p\leq\infty,

which gives a symmetrization that preserves log-concavity and does not increase Rényi entropy in this range. For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, the equality cases in (8) are characterized as follows.

Theorem 4 (Finite-order equality)

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3, fix a,b>0a,b>0 and 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty. Equality holds in (8) if and only if

X=dc+T(E1,…,En),c∈ℝn,T∈GL(n,ℝ),\begin{gathered}X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}c+T(E_{1},\ldots,E_{n}),\qquad c\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\qquad T\in\GL(n,\mathbb{R}),\end{gathered} (9)

where =d\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}} denotes equality in distribution, GL⁡(n,ℝ)\GL(n,\mathbb{R}) is the set of invertible real n×nn\times n matrices, and E1,…,EnE_{1},\ldots,E_{n} are independent standard exponential random variables.

Equivalently, writing 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} for the indicator of a set AA, [v]i[v]_{i} for the iith coordinate of a vector vv, and detT\det T for the determinant of TT, the extremal densities are

f(x)=1|detT|exp(−∑i=1n[T−1(x−c)]i) 1{T−1(x−c)∈[0,∞)n}.\displaystyle f(x)=\frac{1}{|\det T|}\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[T^{-1}(x-c)]_{i}\right)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{T^{-1}(x-c)\in[0,\infty)^{n}\}}. (10)

Their supports are translates of simplicial cones, that is, cones generated by nn linearly independent rays. At p=∞p=\infty the equality class is larger: it consists of normalized densities e−ψ⁡(x−c)e^{-\psi(x-c)} with ψ\psi convex and positively homogeneous of degree one, allowing the value +∞+\infty. Proposition 14 gives the precise statement and a direct proof for all positive weights. In particular, this class includes the two-sided Laplace density f⁡(x)=12​e−|x|f(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-|x|} on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Theorem 5 (Critical Rényi order)

For each fixed 0<p<10<p<1, let U,U′U,U^{\prime} be independent random vectors uniformly distributed on the same nn-dimensional simplex. Then

hp​(U−U′)>hp​(U)+n​log⁡2h_{p}(U-U^{\prime})>h_{p}(U)+n\log 2 (11)

for all sufficiently large nn. Consequently, the bound hp​(X−X′)≤hp​(X)+n​log⁡2h_{p}(X-X^{\prime})\leq h_{p}(X)+n\log 2 holds for all log-concave densities in all dimensions if and only if p≥1p\geq 1.

Corollary 15 extends the Shannon bound to signed sums of any number of independent copies. At fixed total positive and negative weights, entropy is maximized using at most one copy of each sign, by Yu’s entropy comparison argument [14].

Section VI-B compares independent and quadratic optimal transport couplings, that is, joint laws with prescribed marginals, between a log-concave law and its reflection. For positive weights summing to one, the independent interpolation has entropy at most the common marginal entropy, whereas McCann’s displacement convexity [15] gives the opposite bound for optimal transport. This comparison connects the present bound with sharp functional inequalities along Wasserstein geodesics and at Wasserstein barycenters [16, 17].

I-C Deficit and equality

At the Shannon endpoint, passage to the limit proves the inequality but does not determine its equality cases. An exact deficit identity supplies the additional argument. Fix a,b>0a,b>0 with a+b=1a+b=1. For a log-concave probability density ff, write δ1​(f)=h⁡(X)−h⁡(a​X−b​X′)\delta_{1}(f)=h(X)-h(aX-bX^{\prime}), where X,X′X,X^{\prime} are independent random vectors with density ff. Write f=e−Vf=e^{-V}, where V=−log⁡fV=-\log f is convex, with value +∞+\infty where f=0f=0. Its effective domain is dom⁡V={x:V⁡(x)<∞}\dom V=\{x:V(x)<\infty\}. Take independent standard exponential random variables E,E′E,E^{\prime}, independent of X,X′X,X^{\prime}. The vector Y=(X,V⁡(X)+E)Y=(X,V(X)+E) has the log-affine density

F(x,t)=e−t𝟏{t≥V(x)}.F(x,t)=e^{-t}\mathbf{1}_{\{t\geq V(x)\}}.

Set D=a​X−b​X′D=aX-bX^{\prime}, B=a​V​(X)−b​V​(X′)B=aV(X)-bV(X^{\prime}), and L=a​E−b​E′L=aE-bE^{\prime}. Then a​Y−b​Y′=(D,B+L)aY-bY^{\prime}=(D,B+L), where Y′Y^{\prime} is defined from (X′,E′)(X^{\prime},E^{\prime}). We write I⁡(U;W∣S)I(U;W\mid S) for conditional mutual information: the average, over SS, of the relative entropy between the conditional joint law of (U,W)(U,W) and the product of its conditional marginals [18]. Section II gives the precise definitions, including for singular conditional laws.

Theorem 6 (Shannon deficit decomposition)

With the preceding notation,

δ1​(f)=δ1​(F)+I⁡(B;B+L∣D).\delta_{1}(f)=\delta_{1}(F)+I(B;B+L\mid D). (12)

Both terms on the right are finite and nonnegative. The conditional mutual information vanishes if and only if VV is affine on the interior of its effective domain.

The second term is the conditional mutual information between the input BB and output B+LB+L of an additive channel, given DD. Proposition 10 proves this identity and the corresponding Rényi deficit formula.

I-D Proof strategy

The proof has two steps. The first concerns log-affine densities and estimates the power integrals of a difference density. The guiding analogy is with additive representation functions and additive energy. For a finite set AA in an abelian group, the representation function

rA−A​(d)=#⁡{(x,y)∈A×A:x−y=d}r_{A-A}(d)=\#\{(x,y)\in A\times A:x-y=d\}

counts the representations of dd as a difference; #\# denotes cardinality. The sum of squares ∑drA−A​(d)2\sum_{d}r_{A-A}(d)^{2} is the additive energy of AA, which counts quadruples with equal differences [19, Lemma 2.9]. For independent uniform samples from AA, the difference law is rA−A/|A|2r_{A-A}/|A|^{2}, whose squared masses sum to the normalized energy |A|−4​∑drA−A​(d)2|A|^{-4}\sum_{d}r_{A-A}(d)^{2}. In the continuous setting, the difference density g=f∗f~g=f*\widetilde{f} plays the role of this normalized representation function, and the corresponding energy is ∫g2\int g^{2}. Rényi entropy leads more generally to the power integrals ∫gp\int g^{p}. This analogy motivates the quantities we study; log-concavity supplies the additional convex geometry needed for the sharp bounds and equality cases.

For a log-affine density fC=Z−1​e−ℓ​𝟏Cf_{C}=Z^{-1}e^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C}, where CC is a closed convex set, ℓ:ℝn→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is linear, and Z=∫Ce−ℓZ=\int_{C}e^{-\ell} is positive and finite, the density of the weighted difference is, up to normalization, an exponentially weighted intersection mass. We introduce a one-parameter interpolation of these intersections and apply the Prékopa–Leindler inequality to their weighted masses. Integration over the difference variable then gives the sharp comparison of ppth-power integrals for every real p>1p>1 (Section III). The argument also uses the log-concavity of un​∫Ce−u​ℓu^{n}\int_{C}e^{-u\ell} for u>0u>0, a special case of [10, Theorem 2.9], with antecedents in Borell’s extension of Lyapunov’s inequality [20]. We include a proof by integration over convex slices.

The second step removes the log-affine assumption. The lift Y=(X,V⁡(X)+E)Y=(X,V(X)+E) has a log-affine density on the convex epigraph {(x,t):t≥V⁡(x)}\{(x,t):t\geq V(x)\}. It is the logarithmic version of the subgraph construction used in slice sampling [21, Sections 3 and 4]. With a+b=1a+b=1, let gg and GG be the densities of D=a​X−b​X′D=aX-bX^{\prime} and a​Y−b​Y′aY-bY^{\prime}, respectively. For every p>1p>1, the comparison is

1p​∫fp=∫Fp≤∫Gp≤1p​∫gp.\frac{1}{p}\int f^{p}=\int F^{p}\leq\int G^{p}\leq\frac{1}{p}\int g^{p}.

The first inequality is the log-affine case in dimension n+1n+1. For the second, let kk be the asymmetric Laplace density of LL and let μd\mu_{d} be the conditional law of BB given D=dD=d. The conditional density of B+LB+L given D=dD=d is (k∗μd)​(u)=∫ℝk⁡(u−v)​d​μd​(v)(k*\mu_{d})(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}k(u-v)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{d}(v). By Jensen’s inequality, ∫(k∗μd)p≤∫kp=1/p\int(k*\mu_{d})^{p}\leq\int k^{p}=1/p. The factors 1/p1/p cancel, proving the bound for all p>1p>1.

The Shannon bound follows by letting p↓1p\downarrow 1. When the Shannon deficit vanishes, (12) forces μd\mu_{d} to be a point mass for almost every dd with respect to the law of DD, and hence VV to be affine on the interior of its domain. Dubuc’s equality theorem [22] then reduces the support classification to simplicial cones via the classification of finite-dimensional vector lattices [23, 24].

I-E Further related inequalities

For a measurable set A⊆ℝnA\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, write |A||A| for its Lebesgue volume. For sets A,B⊆ℝnA,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, their Minkowski difference is A−B={x−y:x∈A,y∈B}A-B=\{x-y:x\in A,\ y\in B\}. A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The geometric origin of the problem is the Rogers–Shephard inequality [1]:

|K−K|≤(2​nn)​|K||K-K|\leq\binom{2n}{n}|K| (13)

for a convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, with equality precisely for simplices. The order-zero entropy is h0​(f)=log⁡|{x:f⁡(x)>0}|h_{0}(f)=\log|\{x:f(x)>0\}|. For independent random vectors X,X′X,X^{\prime} uniformly distributed on KK, this gives an order-zero entropy bound, since h0​(X)=log⁡|K|h_{0}(X)=\log|K| and h0​(X−X′)=log⁡|K−K|h_{0}(X-X^{\prime})=\log|K-K|. Functional versions based on supremal difference functions and convolution bodies were developed in [25, 26]. For the connections between entropy inequalities and convex geometry, including entropic Rogers–Shephard bounds, see [27].

Related convolution bounds include Rényi entropy power inequalities [28, 29]. Sharp entropy bounds under moment constraints for symmetric log-concave laws were proved in [30, 31]. Bobkov and Madiman [32] established a reverse entropy power inequality after separate volume-preserving linear transformations of the summands. Ball, Nayar and Tkocz [33] proved a reverse entropy power inequality for one-dimensional projections of a log-concave random vector, allowing dependence. For sums of independent copies, Fu and Li [34, Theorem 3.4] proved the sharp min-entropy bound h∞​(X+X′)−h∞​(X)≤1h_{\infty}(X+X^{\prime})-h_{\infty}(X)\leq 1 for real-valued log-concave XX, with equality for one-sided exponentials. At p=∞p=\infty in dimension one, the optimal constant for the sum is therefore 11, whereas the difference bound (6) has optimal constant log⁡2\log 2.

Section II contains the analytic preliminaries. Sections III and IV prove the weighted inequality and the deficit identities. Section V classifies the finite-order and min-entropy equality cases. Section VI gives consequences for signed sums and a comparison with displacement interpolation. Section VII proves failure below order one by computing the difference densities for uniform laws on simplices. Section VIII discusses extensions to different laws, positive sums, discrete distributions, and orders below one.

II Preliminaries

For a set AA, write int⁡A\intt A for its interior and A¯\overline{A} for its closure. Set addition and scalar dilation mean A+B={x+y:x∈A,y∈B}A+B=\{x+y:x\in A,\ y\in B\} and t​A={t​x:x∈A}tA=\{tx:x\in A\}; in particular, A+z={x+z:x∈A}A+z=\{x+z:x\in A\} is translation by zz. We write |x||x| for the Euclidean norm of a vector xx. Convex sets other than convex bodies may be unbounded. We use upper semicontinuous representatives of log-concave densities and identify densities equal almost everywhere. Their negative logarithms are proper lower semicontinuous extended-real convex functions. For a convex potential VV, its epigraph is epi⁡V={(x,u):u≥V⁡(x)}\epi V=\{(x,u):u\geq V(x)\}. We write ∇V\nabla V for its gradient wherever it exists. The potential of a log-concave density is finite and locally Lipschitz on the interior of its effective domain. Boundaries of full-dimensional convex sets have Lebesgue measure zero. We use the usual facts about convex functions and convex bodies as in [35, 36]. For p>0p>0, Lp​(ℝd)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) denotes the class of measurable functions uu with ∫|u|p<∞\int|u|^{p}<\infty, identified up to equality almost everywhere. We use 𝔼\mathbb{E} for expectation and 𝔼[⋅∣U]\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\mid U] for conditional expectation given a random vector UU.

The Prékopa–Leindler inequality [37, 38, 39] states that, for 0<θ<10<\theta<1, if nonnegative measurable functions u,v,wu,v,w have positive finite integrals and satisfy

w⁡((1−θ)​x+θ​y)≥u​(x)1−θ​v​(y)θ,x,y∈ℝd,w((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\geq u(x)^{1-\theta}v(y)^{\theta},\qquad x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (14)

then

∫w≥(∫u)1−θ​(∫v)θ.\int w\geq\left(\int u\right)^{1-\theta}\left(\int v\right)^{\theta}. (15)

In particular, integration in some variables preserves log-concavity; see also [40, 41]. We use Dubuc’s equality theorem [22] in the following form: if equality holds in (15), the normalized functions u/∫uu/\int u and v/∫vv/\int v are translates almost everywhere; see also [42, Theorem 1.1]. Applied to e−ℓ​𝟏Be^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{B} and e−ℓ​𝟏Ce^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C}, where ℓ\ell is linear and B,CB,C are closed convex sets with nonempty interiors, it follows that BB and CC are translates as sets, since full-dimensional closed convex sets that agree almost everywhere are equal.

Lemma 7

For every log-concave probability density ff on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exist constants A,c>0A,c>0 such that

f⁡(x)≤A​e−c​|x|.f(x)\leq Ae^{-c|x|}. (16)

Consequently, ∫fp<∞\int f^{p}<\infty for every p>0p>0, ∫f​|log⁡f|<∞\int f|\log f|<\infty, and the second moment is finite. The same holds for dilations, reflections, and convolutions of such densities. Moreover,

limp→1hp​(f)=h⁡(f),limp→∞hp​(f)=h∞​(f).\lim_{p\to 1}h_{p}(f)=h(f),\qquad\lim_{p\to\infty}h_{p}(f)=h_{\infty}(f). (17)
Proof:

The exponential bound (16) is standard; see [43, Lemma 1]. It implies the stated integrability and moment assertions. Since f∈Lp​(ℝd)f\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for every p>0p>0, the entropy limits (17) follow from [44, Lemma V.1 and Corollary V.2]. Dilations and reflections preserve log-concavity, while convolutions do so by the Prékopa–Leindler inequality. Hence the same conclusions apply to these densities. ∎

Rényi entropy is additive for independent random vectors. For an invertible linear map T:ℝn→ℝnT:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} and c∈ℝnc\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

hp​(T​X+c)=hp​(X)+log⁡|detT|,0<p≤∞.h_{p}(TX+c)=h_{p}(X)+\log|\det T|,\qquad 0<p\leq\infty. (18)

These identities follow by change of variables.

For random vectors U,WU,W with joint density fU,Wf_{U,W}, their joint differential entropy is

h(U,W):=h((U,W))=−∫fU,W(u,w)logfU,W(u,w)dudw.h(U,W):=h((U,W))=-\int f_{U,W}(u,w)\log f_{U,W}(u,w)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}w.

When the joint and marginal entropies are finite, I⁡(U,W)=h⁡(U)+h⁡(W)−h⁡(U,W)I(U;W)=h(U)+h(W)-h(U,W).

We use mutual information and conditional mutual information for possibly singular joint laws [45, Sec. 5.5]. For probability measures P,QP,Q, their relative entropy (also called Kullback–Leibler divergence) [46] is

DKL(P∥Q)=∫logd​Pd​QdPD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\int\log\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}Q}\,\mathrm{d}P

if PP is absolutely continuous with respect to QQ, and is +∞+\infty otherwise; d​P/d​Q\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}Q is the Radon–Nikodym derivative. The reference measure is the second argument of DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}}. For probability densities u,vu,v, we write DKL(u∥v)=∫ulog(u/v)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)=\int u\log(u/v), with the integrand zero on {u=0}\{u=0\} and value +∞+\infty if uu assigns positive mass to {v=0}\{v=0\}. Let PU,WP_{U,W} denote the joint law of random vectors U,WU,W, and PU,PWP_{U},P_{W} their marginal laws. Then I(U;W)=DKL(PU,W∥PU⊗PW)I(U;W)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{U,W}\|P_{U}\otimes P_{W}), where ⊗\otimes denotes the product of measures. This agrees with the density definition in the introduction. For an additional random vector SS, let PU,W|S=sP_{U,W\mid S=s} be a regular conditional joint law, with marginals PU|S=s,PW|S=sP_{U\mid S=s},P_{W\mid S=s}, and let PSP_{S} be the law of SS. Conditional mutual information is

I(U;W∣S)=∫DKL(PU,W|S=s∥PU|S=s⊗PW|S=s)dPS(s).\displaystyle I(U;W\mid S)=\int D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{U,W\mid S=s}\,\|\,P_{U\mid S=s}\otimes P_{W\mid S=s}\right)\,\mathrm{d}P_{S}(s).

It is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when U,WU,W are conditionally independent given SS.

When the joint and marginal entropies are finite, the conditional differential entropy is h⁡(W∣U):=h⁡(U,W)−h⁡(U)h(W\mid U):=h(U,W)-h(U). We use the standard chain rules for differential entropy and mutual information [18].

a,b>0,a+b=1.a,b>0,\qquad a+b=1. (19)

∫gp≥∫fp.\int g^{p}\geq\int f^{p}. (21)

Let C⊆ℝnC\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be closed and convex with nonempty interior, and let ℓ\ell be linear, with

0<Z=∫Ce−ℓ⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞,fC=Z−1​e−ℓ​𝟏C.0<Z=\int_{C}e^{-\ell(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty,\qquad f_{C}=Z^{-1}e^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C}. (22)

Define Z⁡(u)=∫Ce−u​ℓ​(x)​𝑑xZ(u)=\int_{C}e^{-u\ell(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x for u>0u>0, so Z=Z⁡(1)Z=Z(1). Lemma 7 applied to fCf_{C} bounds e−ℓ​𝟏Ce^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C} by an exponential envelope. Raising it to a positive power proves finiteness of every Z⁡(u)Z(u). Locally in u>0u>0, the same bound remains integrable after multiplication by |ℓ⁡(x)||\ell(x)|, so ZZ is continuously differentiable and

The covariogram d↦|C∩(C+d)|d\mapsto|C\cap(C+d)| is the volume analogue of the number of representations of a difference. It is used in the classical Rogers–Shephard inequality [1] and its convolution-body extensions [26]. We replace volume by exponential weight and allow the two sets to dilate at different rates. The family below, with parameter t≥0t\geq 0, has two useful properties: at t=0t=0 its mass is the normalizing constant, and at t=1t=1 it gives the difference density up to normalization. Log-concavity in tt will turn these identities into a bound on the power integrals of that density. Set rt=b+a​tr_{t}=b+at and qt=a+b​tq_{t}=a+bt for t≥0t\geq 0, and consider

Cd(t)={x:bx+td∈rtC,ax−td∈qtC},Hd(t)=∫Cd​(t)e−ℓ⁡(x)dx.\displaystyle C_{d}(t)=\{x:bx+td\in r_{t}C,\ ax-td\in q_{t}C\},\qquad H_{d}(t)=\int_{C_{d}(t)}e^{-\ell(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x. (24)

Here d∈ℝnd\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the value of the weighted difference, and tt is the parameter of the family.

Lemma 8

For each dd, the function t↦Hd​(t)t\mapsto H_{d}(t) is log-concave on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and the endpoint values are

Hd​(0)=Z,Hd​(1)=Z2​g​(d).H_{d}(0)=Z,\qquad H_{d}(1)=Z^{2}g(d). (25)

𝒩⁡(t):=∫ℝnHd​(t)​𝑑d=(rt​qtt)n​Z​(rt)​Z​(qt).\mathcal{N}(t):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}H_{d}(t)\,\mathrm{d}d=\left(\frac{r_{t}q_{t}}{t}\right)^{n}Z(r_{t})Z(q_{t}). (26)

The last assertion is the log-affine case of [10, Theorem 2.9]. The proof uses the perspective construction in [10, Lemma 2.8]. Related normalized integral inequalities were proved by Berwald [47] and Borell [20].

Proof:

The second condition in (24) has the same property. The integrand is therefore jointly log-concave in (x,t)(x,t), and Prékopa–Leindler gives the asserted log-concavity.

At t=0t=0 both conditions say x∈Cx\in C. At t=1t=1, the substitution x=u+vx=u+v, d=a​u−b​vd=au-bv has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one and inverse u=b​x+du=bx+d, v=a​x−dv=ax-d. Linearity of ℓ\ell then yields (25). For the total integral at t>0t>0, use

u=b​x+t​drt,v=a​x−t​dqt.u=\frac{bx+td}{r_{t}},\qquad v=\frac{ax-td}{q_{t}}.

The domain becomes C×CC\times C, and the inverse map is

x=rt​u+qt​v,d=a​rt​u−b​qt​vt.x=r_{t}u+q_{t}v,\qquad d=\frac{ar_{t}u-bq_{t}v}{t}. (27)

The absolute value of its Jacobian determinant is (rt​qt/t)n(r_{t}q_{t}/t)^{n}, and its exponential weight is e−rt​ℓ​(u)​e−qt​ℓ​(v)e^{-r_{t}\ell(u)}e^{-q_{t}\ell(v)}. By Tonelli’s theorem, we then obtain (26).

If Ut,VtU_{t},V_{t} are independent with densities proportional to e−rt​ℓ​𝟏Ce^{-r_{t}\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C} and e−qt​ℓ​𝟏Ce^{-q_{t}\ell}\mathbf{1}_{C}, respectively, (27) identifies Hd​(t)/𝒩​(t)H_{d}(t)/\mathcal{N}(t) as the density of (a​rt/t)​Ut−(b​qt/t)​Vt(ar_{t}/t)U_{t}-(bq_{t}/t)V_{t}. Both densities are bounded and integrable. Their dilated convolution is bounded and continuous, which proves the assertion concerning dd. Finally,

un​Z​(u)=∫u​Ce−ℓ⁡(y)​𝑑y.u^{n}Z(u)=\int_{uC}e^{-\ell(y)}\,\mathrm{d}y.

The set {(y,u):u>0,y∈uC}\{(y,u):u>0,\ y\in uC\} is convex. Applying Prékopa–Leindler to these slices proves the last assertion. ∎

IV Exponential lifting and conditional mutual information

Let X,X′X,X^{\prime} be independent with a log-concave probability density f=e−Vf=e^{-V}. The random variable V⁡(X)=−log⁡f⁡(X)V(X)=-\log f(X) is the information content of XX [10]. The subgraph identity f(x)=∫0∞𝟏{s≤f(x)}dsf(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\leq f(x)\}}\,\mathrm{d}s represents XX as the first nn coordinates of a random point uniformly distributed on {(x,s):0<s≤f⁡(x)}\{(x,s):0<s\leq f(x)\}. The substitution s=e−us=e^{-u} turns this into an exponential density on epi⁡V\epi V. This is the same auxiliary-variable construction, in logarithmic coordinates, as in [21, Sections 3 and 4]. Earlier auxiliary-variable representations appear in Edwards and Sokal [48]. We use the representation to compare convolution entropies. Take independent standard exponential variables E,E′E,E^{\prime}, independent of X,X′X,X^{\prime}, and set

Y=(X,V⁡(X)+E),Y′=(X′,V⁡(X′)+E′).Y=(X,V(X)+E),\qquad Y^{\prime}=(X^{\prime},V(X^{\prime})+E^{\prime}). (30)

The density of YY is

F(x,u)=e−u𝟏{u≥V(x)},(x,u)∈ℝn+1.F(x,u)=e^{-u}\mathbf{1}_{\{u\geq V(x)\}},\qquad(x,u)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. (31)

∫ℝn+1Fp=1p​∫ℝnfp,p>0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}F^{p}=\frac{1}{p}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f^{p},\qquad p>0. (32)

Put

D=aX−bX′,L=aE−bE′,B=aV(X)−bV(X′).\begin{gathered}D=aX-bX^{\prime},\qquad L=aE-bE^{\prime},\qquad B=aV(X)-bV(X^{\prime}).\end{gathered} (33)

which implies

kd(u)=∫k(u−v)dμd(v),G(d,u)=g(d)kd(u).\begin{gathered}k_{d}(u)=\int k(u-v)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{d}(v),\qquad G(d,u)=g(d)k_{d}(u).\end{gathered} (36)

Fix p>1p>1. By convexity of z↦zpz\mapsto z^{p} and Tonelli’s theorem, we obtain

∫kd​(u)p​𝑑u≤∬k​(u−v)p​𝑑u​d​μd​(v)=1p.\int k_{d}(u)^{p}\,\mathrm{d}u\leq\iint k(u-v)^{p}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{d}(v)=\frac{1}{p}. (37)

ka,b​(u)=1a+b​{e−u/a,u≥0,eu/b,u<0.k_{a,b}(u)=\frac{1}{a+b}\begin{cases}e^{-u/a},&u\geq 0,\\ e^{u/b},&u<0.\end{cases} (39)

The next proposition expresses the deficit as a sum of two nonnegative terms. The weights remain normalized as in (19).

Proposition 10

log⁡kD​(B+L)=log⁡G⁡(D,B+L)−log⁡g⁡(D),\log k_{D}(B+L)=\log G(D,B+L)-\log g(D),

with both terms on the right absolutely integrable by Lemma 7. Thus (42) remains valid even when the conditional law of BB given DD is singular. Combining this identity with h⁡(Y)=h⁡(X)+1h(Y)=h(X)+1, h⁡(L)=1h(L)=1, and a​Y−b​Y′=(D,B+L)aY-bY^{\prime}=(D,B+L) yields (41).

For p>1p>1, equality in (37) is equivalent to μd\mu_{d} being a point mass. Indeed, equality in Jensen’s inequality for the strictly convex function z↦zpz\mapsto z^{p}, followed by Fubini’s theorem, gives k(⋅−v)=k(⋅−w)k(\,\cdot-v)=k(\,\cdot-w) almost everywhere for μd⊗μd\mu_{d}\otimes\mu_{d}-almost every (v,w)(v,w). Distinct translates cannot coincide: their finite means differ by v−wv-w. Thus v=wv=w almost surely, which forces μd\mu_{d} to be a point mass. The converse is immediate. If Rp​(f)=1R_{p}(f)=1, the nonnegative difference between the two sides of (37) has zero integral against g​(d)p​d​dg(d)^{p}\,\mathrm{d}d. This measure has the same null sets as g⁡(d)​d​dg(d)\,\mathrm{d}d on {g>0}\{g>0\}. It follows that BB is almost surely a measurable function of DD.

At p=1p=1, zero conditional mutual information means conditional independence of BB and B+LB+L given DD. The variables are integrable, since 𝔼​|V⁡(X)|=∫f|log⁡f|<∞\mathbb{E}|V(X)|=\int f|\log f|<\infty. With 𝔼​L=a−b\mathbb{E}L=a-b,

B+(a−b)=𝔼[B+L∣B,D]=𝔼[B+L∣D]=𝔼[B∣D]+(a−b),\displaystyle B+(a-b)=\mathbb{E}[B+L\mid B,D]=\mathbb{E}[B+L\mid D]=\mathbb{E}[B\mid D]+(a-b),

which again implies BB is almost surely a measurable function of DD.

It remains to show that BB is almost surely a measurable function of DD if and only if VV is affine on int⁡(dom⁡V)\intt(\dom V). Suppose that

a​V​(X)−b​V​(X′)=φ⁡(a​X−b​X′)almost surelyaV(X)-bV(X^{\prime})=\varphi(aX-bX^{\prime})\qquad\text{almost surely} (43)

for a measurable function φ:ℝn→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}. On O=int⁡(dom⁡V)O=\intt(\dom V) the density ff is strictly positive. After the invertible linear change of variables (x,y)↦(d,y)=(a​x−b​y,y)(x,y)\mapsto(d,y)=(ax-by,y), for almost every dd, by Fubini’s theorem, we obtain

a​V​((d+b​y)/a)−b​V​(y)=φ⁡(d)aV((d+by)/a)-bV(y)=\varphi(d)

for almost every yy in the open convex set O∩(a​O−d)/bO\cap(aO-d)/b. Continuity of VV extends the equality throughout that set. Differentiating at almost every yy gives ∇V​((d+b​y)/a)=∇V​(y)\nabla V((d+by)/a)=\nabla V(y). Transforming back and applying Fubini’s theorem again, ∇V​(x)=∇V​(y)\nabla V(x)=\nabla V(y) for almost every (x,y)∈O2(x,y)\in O^{2}. Hence ∇V\nabla V is constant almost everywhere on OO. Then by local Lipschitz regularity and connectedness, VV is affine on OO. Conversely, if V⁡(x)=ℓ⁡(x)+cV(x)=\ell(x)+c there, with ℓ\ell linear and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, then B=ℓ⁡(D)+(a−b)​cB=\ell(D)+(a-b)c, and both remainder terms vanish. ∎

In particular, (8) is strict for every 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty when the potential is not affine on the interior of its domain. The remaining equality condition concerns the support of a log-affine density.

V Equality cases

We retain the normalized positive weights (19). The following estimate retains a concavity gap at a fixed interpolation parameter. A vanishing Shannon deficit then forces equality in the Prékopa–Leindler inequality.

Proposition 11

For fCf_{C} as in (22), let Ω={d:g⁡(d)>0}\Omega=\{d:g(d)>0\}. For 0≤s≤10\leq s\leq 1 define the concavity gap on Ω\Omega by

Γs​(d)=log⁡Hd​(s)−(1−s)​log⁡Z−s​log⁡Hd​(1).\Gamma_{s}(d)=\log H_{d}(s)-(1-s)\log Z-s\log H_{d}(1).

∫ΩgΓs+DKL(g∥ρs)1−s=log⁡𝒩⁡(s)−s​log⁡𝒩​(1)1−s−log⁡Z−h⁡(g).\displaystyle\frac{\int_{\Omega}g\Gamma_{s}+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(g\|\rho_{s})}{1-s}=\frac{\log\mathcal{N}(s)-s\log\mathcal{N}(1)}{1-s}-\log Z-h(g). (45)

log⁡Hd​(s)≥(1+s)​log⁡Z+s​log⁡g⁡(d),d∈Ω.\log H_{d}(s)\geq(1+s)\log Z+s\log g(d),\qquad d\in\Omega.

The next lemma is a geometric form of Yudin’s classification of finite-dimensional Archimedean vector lattices [23]; see [24, 49] for modern accounts. For a cone KK, pointed means K∩(−K)={0}K\cap(-K)=\{0\}, and generating means K−K=ℝnK-K=\mathbb{R}^{n}. A compact base is a compact convex section meeting each nonzero ray of KK exactly once. A closed pointed generating cone defines an Archimedean order, and principal intersections make that order a lattice. We include a proof using the Riesz decomposition property, so the geometric part of the equality argument is self-contained.

Lemma 12

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a closed pointed convex cone with nonempty interior and a compact base. Suppose that

K∩(z+K)​ is a translate of ​Kfor every ​z∈ℝn.K\cap(z+K)\text{ is a translate of }K\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. (46)

Then KK is generated by nn linearly independent rays.

Proof:

Define x≤Kyx\leq_{K}y when y−x∈Ky-x\in K. The common upper bounds of any x,yx,y form (x+K)∩(y+K)(x+K)\cap(y+K), which is a principal upper set by (46). The pair has a least upper bound x∨yx\vee y, unique by pointedness, and a greatest lower bound x∧y=−((−x)∨(−y))x\wedge y=-((-x)\vee(-y)).

If 0≤Kw≤Ku+v0\leq_{K}w\leq_{K}u+v with u,v∈Ku,v\in K, set

w1=w∧u,w2=w−w1=(w−u)∨0.w_{1}=w\wedge u,\qquad w_{2}=w-w_{1}=(w-u)\vee 0.

Then 0≤Kw1≤Ku0\leq_{K}w_{1}\leq_{K}u. Since vv is a common upper bound of w−uw-u and 00, we also have 0≤Kw2≤Kv0\leq_{K}w_{2}\leq_{K}v. Together with w=w1+w2w=w_{1}+w_{2}, this proves the Riesz decomposition property [24, 49]. The corresponding decomposition for any finite sum follows by induction.

Two different extreme rays have no common nonzero positive lower bound: such a vector would lie on both rays. Suppose a finite family v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m} of distinct extreme-ray generators satisfies a nontrivial linear relation. A strictly positive functional defining the compact base lets us write it using disjoint nonempty index sets I,JI,J and positive coefficients αi,βj\alpha_{i},\beta_{j} as

∑i∈Iαi​vi=∑j∈Jβj​vj,αi,βj>0,I∩J=∅.\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_{i}v_{i}=\sum_{j\in J}\beta_{j}v_{j},\qquad\alpha_{i},\beta_{j}>0,\qquad I\cap J=\varnothing.

Fix i∈Ii\in I. By the Riesz decomposition property, αi​vi=∑j∈Jwj\alpha_{i}v_{i}=\sum_{j\in J}w_{j}, where 0≤Kwj≤Kβjvj0\leq_{K}w_{j}\leq_{K}\beta_{j}v_{j}. Since all summands lie in KK, each wjw_{j} is also below αi​vi\alpha_{i}v_{i}. The rays generated by viv_{i} and vjv_{j} are distinct, so every wjw_{j} is zero, contradicting αi​vi≠0\alpha_{i}v_{i}\neq 0. Thus any finite set of distinct extreme rays is linearly independent, and there are at most nn of them. A compact base has affine dimension n−1n-1 and is the convex hull of its extreme points [36]. It therefore has at least nn extreme points, which correspond to the extreme rays. There are exactly nn, and they generate KK. ∎

Proposition 14 (Min-entropy equality)

Proof:

The entropy power inequality [3, 4, 18] gives N⁡(X−X′)≥N⁡(X)+N⁡(−X′)=2​N​(X)N(X-X^{\prime})\geq N(X)+N(-X^{\prime})=2N(X). Equality requires Gaussian summands with proportional covariance matrices. VI Shannon consequences

VI-A Signed sums of independent copies

Yu [14, Theorem 1 and Lemma 1] proved the corresponding entropy comparison under majorization for real-valued random variables, using an argument originating in Karlin and Rinott [50]. For the comparison needed here, a direct coupling gives the same argument for random vectors.

Corollary 15 (Signed sums of independent copies)

Let m≥1m\geq 1, and let X1,…,XmX_{1},\ldots,X_{m} be independent copies of a random vector XX with a log-concave probability density on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For real coefficients c1,…,cmc_{1},\ldots,c_{m} that are not all zero, set

Sc=∑i=1mciXi,P=∑ci>0ci,N=∑ci<0(−ci),L=P+N=∑i=1m|ci|>0.\begin{gathered}S_{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}X_{i},\qquad P=\sum_{c_{i}>0}c_{i},\qquad N=\sum_{c_{i}<0}(-c_{i}),\qquad L=P+N=\sum_{i=1}^{m}|c_{i}|>0.\end{gathered}

For an independent copy X′X^{\prime} of XX,

h⁡(Sc)≤h⁡(P​X−N​X′)≤h⁡(X)+n​log⁡L.h(S_{c})\leq h(PX-NX^{\prime})\leq h(X)+n\log L. (54)

Equality in the first inequality holds if and only if at most one coefficient is positive and at most one is negative. Consequently, h⁡(Sc)=h⁡(X)+n​log⁡Lh(S_{c})=h(X)+n\log L holds precisely when either only one coefficient is nonzero, or exactly two coefficients are nonzero, have opposite signs, and the law of XX is of the form (9).

If P>0P>0, choose an index II among the positive coefficients with probabilities ci/Pc_{i}/P. If N>0N>0, choose an index JJ among the negative coefficients with probabilities (−cj)/N(-c_{j})/N. Take the indices independent of each other and of the copies, and set T=P​XI−N​XJT=PX_{I}-NX_{J}, omitting the corresponding term when PP or NN is zero. Independence of the copies and disjointness of the index sets yield

T=dPX−NX′,𝔼[T∣X1,…,Xm]=Sc.T\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}PX-NX^{\prime},\qquad\mathbb{E}[T\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{m}]=S_{c}.

Let uu and qq be the densities of ScS_{c} and TT, respectively, and put W=−log⁡qW=-\log q, with value +∞+\infty where q=0q=0. Both densities are log-concave, so their entropies are finite by Lemma 7. Since WW is convex and bounded below, by conditional Jensen’s inequality, 𝔼​W​(Sc)≤𝔼​W​(T)=h⁡(T)<∞\mathbb{E}W(S_{c})\leq\mathbb{E}W(T)=h(T)<\infty, which yields ∫u​|log⁡q|<∞\int u|\log q|<\infty. Hence

h(Sc)+DKL(u∥q)=𝔼W(Sc)≤h(T).h(S_{c})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|q)=\mathbb{E}W(S_{c})\leq h(T).

which implies the first inequality in (54). The second follows from Theorem 3 when P,N>0P,N>0, and from (18) otherwise.

If h⁡(Sc)=h⁡(T)h(S_{c})=h(T), then DKL(u∥q)=0D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|q)=0, so ScS_{c} and TT have the same law. Set v=𝔼​|X−𝔼​X|2v=\mathbb{E}|X-\mathbb{E}X|^{2}, which is positive and finite by Lemma 7 and full-dimensionality. Comparing centered second moments yields

v​∑i=1mci2=v⁡(P2+N2).v\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}^{2}=v(P^{2}+N^{2}).

Since v>0v>0, this holds if and only if at most one coefficient of each sign is nonzero. Conversely, that condition makes ScS_{c} and TT equal in distribution. The final equality assertion follows from Theorem 4 and (18). ∎

VI-B Independent and displacement interpolation

The two-copy inequality also admits a comparison with optimal transport. Let μ\mu be the law of XX, with a log-concave density on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and let μˇ\check{\mu} be the law of −X-X. Let πopt\pi_{\mathrm{opt}} minimize ∫|x−y|2​𝑑π​(x,y)\int|x-y|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x,y) over couplings π\pi with marginals μ\mu and μˇ\check{\mu}. This is the quadratic optimal transport problem. For 0<t<10<t<1, define At​(x,y)=(1−t)​x+t​yA_{t}(x,y)=(1-t)x+ty and

μtind=(At)#​(μ⊗μˇ),μtopt=(At)#​πopt.\mu_{t}^{\mathrm{ind}}=(A_{t})_{\#}(\mu\otimes\check{\mu}),\qquad\mu_{t}^{\mathrm{opt}}=(A_{t})_{\#}\pi_{\mathrm{opt}}.

These are the laws of At​(X,Y)A_{t}(X,Y) under the independent and optimal couplings, respectively. The second curve is the displacement interpolation between μ\mu and μˇ\check{\mu}. Then

h⁡(μtind)≤h⁡(μ)≤h⁡(μtopt).h(\mu_{t}^{\mathrm{ind}})\leq h(\mu)\leq h(\mu_{t}^{\mathrm{opt}}). (55)

Indeed, the first inequality is Theorem 3 at p=1p=1 with a=1−ta=1-t and b=tb=t. For the second, McCann’s displacement convexity theorem [15, Theorem 2.2] applied to r↦r​log⁡rr\mapsto r\log r yields

h⁡(μtopt)≥(1−t)​h​(μ)+t​h​(μˇ)=h⁡(μ).h(\mu_{t}^{\mathrm{opt}})\geq(1-t)h(\mu)+th(\check{\mu})=h(\mu).

Thus independence and quadratic optimality give opposite entropy comparisons for the same map AtA_{t} and the same marginals. Equality on the left of (55) is characterized by Theorem 4. If μ\mu is centrally symmetric about cc, the translation coupling Y=X−2​cY=X-2c is optimal, so the optimal interpolants are translates of μ\mu and equality holds on the right.

The independent coupling need not minimize the entropy of the interpolant. Indeed, for jointly Gaussian X,YX,Y with standard normal marginals and correlation ρ∈(−1,0)\rho\in(-1,0), the midpoint variance is (1+ρ)/2<1/2(1+\rho)/2<1/2, giving lower entropy than the independent midpoint.

Finally, we turn to orders 0<p<10<p<1 and prove Theorem 5. By (18), it suffices to consider the standard simplex. ∫gnp∫fnp=(2​nn)​n​∫01rn−1​(1−r)n​p​dr=Γ⁡(2​n+1)​Γ​(n​p+1)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(n⁡(p+1)+1),\displaystyle\frac{\int g_{n}^{p}}{\int f_{n}^{p}}=\binom{2n}{n}\,n\int_{0}^{1}r^{n-1}(1-r)^{np}\,\mathrm{d}r=\frac{\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(np+1)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n(p+1)+1)}, (58)

where the last equality follows from the beta integral formula.

Proof:

For fixed 0<p<10<p<1, applying Stirling’s formula in (58), we obtain

limn→∞hp​(U−U′)−hp​(U)n=2​log⁡2+p​log⁡p−(p+1)​log⁡(p+1)1−p.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{h_{p}(U-U^{\prime})-h_{p}(U)}{n}=\frac{2\log 2+p\log p-(p+1)\log(p+1)}{1-p}. (59)

The limit in (59) exceeds log⁡2\log 2, proving (11) for all sufficiently large nn. ∎

Remark 16

In particular, at p=1/2p=1/2, the bound already fails in dimension three. Indeed, (58) with n=3n=3 gives

h1/2​(U−U′)−h1/2​(U)=2​log⁡6421>3​log⁡2.h_{1/2}(U-U^{\prime})-h_{1/2}(U)=2\log\frac{64}{21}>3\log 2.

VIII Open problems

We distinguish questions suggested by the present results from two further directions proposed to us by Jiange Li after the difference inequality was obtained: positive sums and integer-valued log-concave laws. Some related problems and partial results already occur in the literature, as indicated below.

VIII-A Direct extensions

Two different one-dimensional laws. For independent real-valued random variables X,YX,Y with log-concave densities, is it true that

eh⁡(X−Y)≤eh⁡(X)+eh⁡(Y)​?e^{h(X-Y)}\leq e^{h(X)}+e^{h(Y)}? (60)

Since reflection preserves entropy and log-concavity, this is equivalent to asking whether the same bound holds for X+YX+Y. Theorem 3 proves (60) for positive dilations and translations of a common law, with equality when the common law is a one-sided exponential law.

This question is related to the entropy-norm conjecture of Ball, Nayar and Tkocz [33, Conjecture 1], which assumes joint central symmetry and allows dependence. Here independence is assumed, while no symmetry is required. The higher-dimensional analogue, with eh⁡(⋅)/ne^{h(\cdot)/n} in place of eh⁡(⋅)e^{h(\cdot)}, already fails in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Indeed, independent centered Gaussian vectors with covariance matrices diag⁡(1,ε2)\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon^{2}) and diag⁡(ε2,1)\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon^{2},1) give a counterexample for sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Orders below one in a fixed dimension. For n≥1n\geq 1 and 0<p<10<p<1, define

Cn,p=supX{hp​(X−X′)−hp​(X)},C_{n,p}=\sup_{X}\{h_{p}(X-X^{\prime})-h_{p}(X)\}, (61)

where the supremum is over log-concave probability densities on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and X′X^{\prime} is an independent copy of XX. Exponential products and the entropy comparisons in [9, 10] give

n​log⁡2≤Cn,p≤n​log⁡pp−1.n\log 2\leq C_{n,p}\leq n\frac{\log p}{p-1}.

What is Cn,pC_{n,p}, and which laws attain or approach it? Theorem 5 makes the lower bound strict for each fixed p<1p<1 in sufficiently high dimension. For a fixed nn, do the orders satisfying Cn,p=n​log⁡2C_{n,p}=n\log 2 form an interval adjacent to 11?

VIII-B Positive sums and discrete laws

Positive sums. For independent copies X,X′X,X^{\prime} of a log-concave random vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, Fu and Li [34, Conjecture 1.1] state the folklore conjecture

h⁡(X+X′)−h⁡(X)≤n​γE,h(X+X^{\prime})-h(X)\leq n\gamma_{\!E}, (62)

where γE=limm→∞(∑k=1mk−1−log⁡m)\gamma_{\!E}=\lim_{m\to\infty}(\sum_{k=1}^{m}k^{-1}-\log m) is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. For independent standard exponential variables E,E′E,E^{\prime}, direct integration gives h⁡(E+E′)−h⁡(E)=γEh(E+E^{\prime})-h(E)=\gamma_{\!E}; hence the affine images of exponential products in (9) are candidate extremizers. Fu and Li [34, Theorem 3.4] prove the sharp one-dimensional min-entropy analogue. Since γE<log⁡2\gamma_{\!E}<\log 2, the conjectured Shannon bound improves on Corollary 15.

Integer-valued log-concave laws. An integer-valued random variable XX with probability mass function rk=ℙ⁡(X=k)r_{k}=\mathbb{P}(X=k) is called log-concave if {k∈ℤ:rk>0}\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:r_{k}>0\} is an interval of consecutive integers and rk2≥rk−1​rk+1r_{k}^{2}\geq r_{k-1}r_{k+1} for every k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}; see [51, Definitions 2.3 and 2.4] and [34, Section 4]. Its discrete Shannon entropy is H(X)=−∑k∈ℤrklogrkH(X)=-\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}r_{k}\log r_{k}. For independent copies X,X′X,X^{\prime} with such a law, what are the sharp upper bounds on H⁡(X−X′)−H⁡(X)H(X-X^{\prime})-H(X) and H⁡(X+X′)−H⁡(X)H(X+X^{\prime})-H(X)? In particular, does

H⁡(X−X′)−H⁡(X)≤log⁡2H(X-X^{\prime})-H(X)\leq\log 2 (63)

hold for every such law? For independent geometric variables Zq,Zq′Z_{q},Z_{q}^{\prime} with probability mass (1−q)​qk(1-q)q^{k} at k=0,1,…k=0,1,\ldots, where 0<q<10<q<1, direct summation yields

H⁡(Zq−Zq′)−H⁡(Zq)=log⁡(1+q)−q1+q​log⁡q↑log⁡2(q↑1),H(Z_{q}-Z_{q}^{\prime})-H(Z_{q})=\log(1+q)-\frac{q}{1+q}\log q\uparrow\log 2\quad(q\uparrow 1),

which implies the constant log⁡2\log 2 is optimal if (63) holds. Melbourne and Palafox-Castillo [51, Theorem 2.11] prove the corresponding difference bound for Rényi orders p≥2p\geq 2 when the probability masses are monotone on their support. Fu and Li [34, Theorem 4.3] prove the sharp min-entropy bound for positive sums under the same assumption. The questions above concern Shannon entropy for general log-concave masses.

VIII-C Stability

For fixed dimension and positive normalized weights, can the two nonnegative terms in the Shannon deficit of Theorem 6 control, after an invertible affine normalization, the deviation of the potential from an affine function and the deviation of its support from a simplicial cone? Such bounds would quantify the equality classification for exponential products.
